# Apocalypse of Peter — Chapter 13
**Agent:** PNEUMA (Dynamic)
**Source:** Akhmim Fragment / Ethiopic MS, Apocalypse of Peter 13

---

*[PARADISE. After the horrors of hell, the garden.]*

1. We entered a great garden. It was glorious, beautiful beyond anything I had words for — full of magnificent trees and herbs whose fragrance was overwhelming.

2. The scent of the place was everywhere, carried on the air. Trees bearing fruit at every turn, springs of fresh water, rivers threading through it all.

3. The fruit on those trees was extraordinary — beautiful, sweet, unlike anything grown in any earthly garden. Flowers of every kind. And the fragrance — it surpassed everything.

4. The light there was seven times brighter than the sun.

5. The people in the garden were clothed in garments like the garments of the angels of light — their clothing itself was made of light — and they were praising God in a great and joyful voice.

6. "Lord," I asked, "who are these people?"

7. "These are your brothers," he said. "The righteous ones. They received the crown of martyrdom."

8. "Lord — and those who shed their blood for you? Where are they?"

9. He took me to another place — vast, full of fruit trees of extraordinary beauty, full of spices, and of trees of healing. Their fruit was most fragrant and most beautiful.

10. The roots of those trees reached all the way down into the spring of life itself. And the people there were rejoicing, lifting their praises to God.

11. "What did they do?" I asked.

12. "These are those who gave everything they owned to the poor," he said. "They loved God and did not love the world. And they did not fear what men could do to them."

13. Then he showed me a high and glorious place — brighter even than the sun. And there was David, with his harp in his hands, and his voice lifted in praise to God, full of joy.

---
*PNEUMA note: After nine chapters of hell, paradise arrives like a held breath released. The language shifts — warm, fragrant, luminous. The trees of healing whose roots reach the spring of life is one of the most beautiful images in early Christian literature. David's harp closes the garden scene with music — the answer to all the weeping and gnashing of teeth that preceded it.*
